paragraphs: The government is on a small scale what the body politic that contains it is on a large one. It is a moral person endowed with certain faculties, active like the Sovereign and passive like the State, and it can be broken down into other similar relations. This gives rise to a new proportion, and within it yet another, according to the arrangement of the magistracies, until an indivisible middle term is reached, _i.e._ a single ruler or supreme magistrate, who may be represented, in the midst of this progression, as the unity between the fractional and the ordinal series.

Without burdening ourselves with this multiplication of terms, let us be content to regard government as a new body within the State, distinct from the people and the Sovereign, and intermediate between them.

There is an essential difference between these two bodies: the State exists by itself, and the government exists only through the Sovereign. Thus the dominant will of the prince is, or should be, nothing but the general will or the law. His force is only the public force concentrated in his hands, and as soon as he tries to base any absolute and independent act on his own authority, the tie that binds the whole together begins to loosen. Finally, suppose the prince should come to have a particular will more active than the will of the Sovereign, and should use the public force in his hands to obey this particular will. There would then be, so to speak, two Sovereigns, one rightful and the other actual; the social union would vanish at once, and the body politic would be dissolved.

However, for the government to have a true existence and a real life that distinguishes it from the body of the State, and for all its members to be able to act in concert and fulfill the purpose for which it was set up, it must have a particular personality, a sensibility common to its members, and a force and will of its own for its preservation. This particular existence implies assemblies, councils, a power of deliberation and decision, and rights, titles and privileges belonging exclusively to the prince, which make the office of magistrate more honorable in proportion as it is more troublesome. The difficulty lies in how to order this subordinate whole within the whole so that it in no way alters the general constitution by asserting itself. It must always distinguish its own particular force, which is meant to help preserve itself, from the public force, which is meant to preserve the State. In a word, it must always be ready to sacrifice the government to the people, and never the people to the government.

Furthermore, although the artificial body of the government is the work of another artificial body, and has, we may say, only a borrowed and subordinate life, this does not prevent it from acting with more or less vigor or promptness, or from being, so to speak, in more or less robust health. Finally, without departing directly from the purpose for which it was instituted, it may stray more or less from it, depending on how it is constituted.

From all these differences arise the various relations that the government ought to bear to the body of the State, according to the accidental and particular relations by which the State itself is modified. For often the government that is best in itself will become the most harmful if the relations in which it stands have changed according to the defects of the body politic to which it belongs.
